common_name: Casselman Plum (Dark Red-Skinned California Japanese Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Casselman needs a compatible Japanese plum pollinator such as Santa Rosa or Methley nearby, and its roughly 400-500 hour chill requirement places it on the upper edge of what a typical Gulf Coast zone 9a winter reliably supplies.

directions: Casselman emerged from the same mid-twentieth-century California breeding effort that produced Santa Rosa, Friar, and Laroda, and it shares their combination of vigorous growth and heavy, reliable cropping. The medium-to-large fruit ripens to a deep red skin over firm, juicy, amber flesh with a sweet flavor and mild acidity, and it hangs well on the tree without softening quickly, which is useful in humid climates where fruit rot pressure is high. Plant a second compatible plum within about 50 feet for pollination and thin the crop early if it sets heavily, since Casselman is a prolific bearer that can overproduce small fruit. Harvest when the skin colors fully but the flesh still gives slightly to thumb pressure.

common_name: Simka Plum (Large Dark-Skinned Amber-Fleshed Japanese Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Simka is often listed as needing a Santa Rosa-type pollinator nearby and shares Santa Rosa's moderate chill requirement, making it a reasonable fit for the milder parts of zone 9.

directions: Simka produces some of the largest fruit of any common Japanese plum, with a dark maroon-purple skin covering firm amber flesh that is sweet and only mildly tart. Because it is only partially self-fruitful, plant it alongside Santa Rosa or another mid-season Japanese plum to ensure a full crop. The tree is vigorous and needs early, deliberate thinning to prevent limb breakage under a heavy fruit load, and its large fruit size makes it a favorite for fresh eating out of hand. Harvest when the deep color has developed fully over the entire fruit and the flesh yields slightly to gentle pressure.

common_name: Gaviota Plum (Early-Season Dark-Skinned California Japanese Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Gaviota needs a compatible Japanese plum pollinator nearby and ripens early in the season, which in the Gulf South typically means late spring rather than the early-summer timing seen in California.

directions: Gaviota is a University of California-bred Japanese plum valued for ripening well ahead of Santa Rosa while still delivering good size and flavor. The medium-to-large fruit has dark red-black skin over firm, amber-yellow flesh with a rich sweet-tart balance. Plant with another early to mid-season Japanese plum for cross-pollination, and thin fruit clusters to a hand's width apart to encourage larger size and reduce limb stress. Because it ripens early, it is a useful choice for extending the fresh plum harvest window before later varieties like Friar or Elephant Heart come in.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Redheart benefits from a compatible plum pollinator nearby and is an older, widely adaptable selection that has long been grown in home orchards across a range of climates, including the warmer South.

directions: Redheart is an old American-bred plum grown chiefly for its striking deep red flesh, which runs from skin to pit rather than staying pale like most dessert plums. The flavor is sweet with a pleasant tang, and the vivid color makes it especially good for jams, jellies, and preserves that keep their color when cooked. It is a vigorous, reliably productive tree that tolerates a wide range of soils as long as drainage is good. Site with another plum for best pollination and fruit set, and thin the crop if it sets heavily to improve fruit size.

common_name: Bradshaw Plum (Large Purple Heirloom European Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Bradshaw is a European plum with a chill requirement well above what the Gulf Coast typically provides, so it performs best in cooler zones and is included here for gardeners in the northern edge of zone 9 or shipping to cooler-climate relatives.

directions: Bradshaw is a long-cultivated European plum dating to the early nineteenth century, prized for its large, oval, reddish-purple fruit and juicy, yellow, freestone flesh. It is mostly self-fertile but crops more heavily with a second European plum nearby. The tree is vigorous and productive, with fruit that is good fresh, canned, or cooked into jam, though it needs substantially more winter chill than Japanese plum types and struggles in mild-winter climates. Thin fruit if the crop is heavy and prune in late winter to maintain an open center for good light penetration and airflow.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Bluefre is a high-chill European prune plum bred at Michigan State University, better suited to cooler climates than the Gulf Coast, where its chill requirement is unlikely to be reliably met.

directions: Bluefre is a European prune-type plum, a cross of President and Stanley developed to ripen later in the season than either parent. The fruit is large for a prune plum, with dark blue skin, firm greenish-amber flesh, and a rich, sweet flavor good for fresh eating, canning, and drying. It is self-fertile, so a single tree will bear, though yields improve with a second European plum nearby. Prune to an open center in late winter and thin fruit if the crop sets heavily to keep fruit size up and limbs from breaking.

common_name: Valor Plum (Productive Blue-Skinned Canadian Prune Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Valor was bred at Ontario's Vineland research station for a cool-summer, cold-winter climate, so its high chill requirement makes it a poor match for the Gulf Coast even though it is a widely sold garden variety further north.

directions: Valor is a Canadian-bred European prune plum known for heavy, reliable production and large, blue-black fruit with sweet amber flesh. It ripens later than Stanley, giving a late-summer harvest for jam, baking, or fresh eating out of hand. The tree is self-fertile but benefits from a second European plum for a fuller set, and its vigorous growth means it needs annual pruning to keep the canopy open. Thin the fruit if it sets a heavy crop, since Valor is prone to overbearing, which can reduce fruit size in a given year.
sources: Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs

common_name: Early Laxton Plum (Early-Ripening English Gage-Type Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Early Laxton is an English heritage plum bred for a cool maritime climate, and its chill needs make it best suited to cooler zones than the Gulf Coast.

directions: Early Laxton was raised by the English fruit-breeding firm Laxton Brothers and is valued for ripening well ahead of most other European plums, filling the gap before the main dessert-plum season begins. The medium, yellow fruit is flushed with red and has a rich, gage-like sweetness when fully ripe. It is self-fertile, so a lone tree will crop, though yields are fuller with a second plum nearby. Because it ripens early and the blossom appears early too, site it away from frost pockets to protect the flowers from late cold snaps, and thin fruit if the set is heavy to improve size.

common_name: Bavay's Green Gage (Reine Claude de Bavay, Late-Season European Gage Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; this nineteenth-century Belgian gage needs substantial winter chill and cool summer nights to develop its full flavor, making it a better fit for cooler climates than the humid Gulf Coast.

directions: Bavay's Green Gage is a nineteenth-century Belgian selection from the greengage family, ripening several weeks later than the classic Reine Claude and holding its fruit on the tree longer without dropping. The medium, round fruit has yellow-green skin and very sweet, richly flavored flesh considered among the finest of the late gages for fresh eating. It is largely self-fertile but crops more heavily with another European plum nearby for cross-pollination. Prune to an open center after harvest and thin fruit if the set is heavy, since gages tend toward small fruit size when overcropped.

common_name: Purple Gage (Reine Claude Violette, Aromatic Purple-Skinned French Gage Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; this classic French gage needs a cooler winter and summer than the Gulf Coast typically provides, so it is best suited to more temperate growing regions.

directions: Purple Gage, or Reine Claude Violette, is a long-grown French dessert plum distinguished from the classic green Reine Claude by its dusky purple-red skin over sweet, richly aromatic, amber flesh. It is one of the most intensely flavored of the gage plums, prized in France for eating fresh and for preserves. Largely self-fertile, it still benefits from a second European plum planted nearby for a fuller crop. Thin the fruit if it sets heavily to keep the characteristically small gage fruit from becoming undersized, and prune in late winter to maintain an open, airy canopy.

common_name: Hunza Apricot (Drought-Tolerant Heirloom Apricot from the Karakoram)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Hunza has a comparatively low chill requirement and good heat tolerance, but Gulf Coast humidity and spring rains raise brown rot and fruit-set risk more than in its native dry mountain climate.

directions: Hunza apricot originates from the arid Hunza Valley of the Karakoram range in northern Pakistan, where apricots are a dietary staple traditionally dried whole with the sweet, edible kernel left inside the pit. The small-to-medium fruit is sweet, richly flavored, and freestone, and the tree is notably drought-tolerant once established, reflecting its origins in a dry mountain climate. It is self-fertile, so a single tree bears fruit, though a second apricot nearby can improve set in a marginal year. In humid climates like the Gulf South, prioritize excellent drainage and airflow to reduce fungal disease pressure that this variety does not encounter in its native range.

common_name: Autumn Glo Apricot (Very Low-Chill Late-Ripening Apricot)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Autumn Glo has a very low chill requirement of roughly 300 hours and, unusually for an apricot, ripens quite late in the season, which can help it dodge some of the spring frost risk that threatens earlier-blooming low-chill types.

directions: Autumn Glo is a Zaiger Genetics apricot bred specifically for mild-winter regions, combining a very low chill requirement with an unusually late ripening window that stretches the apricot season well past the early-summer finish of most low-chill types. Fruit is medium-sized with attractive orange-blushed skin and sweet, aromatic flesh. The tree is self-fruitful and does not need a separate pollinator. Because it still blooms earlier than most other fruit trees even with its later harvest, site it away from frost pockets, and thin fruit if it sets heavily to keep fruit size and quality up.
